title: Iconic '60s Rock Band Leads the Charge to Make Concert Tickets Affordable Again - NewsBreak
text:
By Sabina Graves ,
3 hours ago
It's no secret that concert tickets have gotten too expensive for the average music fan. Top tours have gone from $84 bucks a seat to more than $130 today, with many major artists selling out stadiums with tickets pushing well past $200 a seat. This writer recently paid around 300 bucks for a pit ticket at the Backstreet Boys Sphere engagement, and that's a legacy boy band. And considering that's nothing for Taylor Swift and Beyoncé fans who notoriously pay hundreds of dollars, it says something about the state of affordability in live music travel.
Related: Concert-Goers Won't Get Turned Away With These Stadium-Approved Bags, All Under $15 at Amazon
Between scalpers and surge pricing, it's felt like a losing game for fans, but one legendary music act has quietly fought against the changing tides for over a decade. Take this classic rock fan's account of purchasing The Rolling Stones tickets as part of their "Lucky Dip" program: "We handed over our tickets to the ticket booth. The customer service rep clicked a few buttons before handing us wristbands. The wristbands said, 'pit, right.'"
They continued their account of their concert experience on Medium, and expressed, "Holy #$%^!" at their shock of the surprise of having purchased these mystery seat tickets and scoring big.
The blog explained, "The Rolling Stones have a brilliant group of tickets called Lucky Dip. There are a small number of tickets released for every show. You are not given a seat in the arena until the day of the show. It can be anywhere in the building. When we saw Rolling Stones in 2012, we got these tickets and were seated up in the nosebleed section. We were fully expecting the tickets to be in worse seats than the ones we had together." They wrote, describing the gamble from the iconic music acts initiative: you get a two-ticket limit, but won't know where you're seated until the show. It could be the nosebleeds or in the pit.
At 20 to 30 bucks a pop, buying these mystery tickets is a worthwhile chance to take, and now more music acts are following The Rolling Stones' lead. Take, for instance, Coldplay , which, according to Jared Braverman via T he Wall Street Journal , the senior vice president of global touring at Live Nation, confirmed they were directly inspired by the Stones and began to offer "Infinity Tickets," which offer their legion of fans a chance to be seated randomly at around $20 a show to “make their show more accessible and more affordable."
Related: This Early-Aughts Rock Star Thought About Quitting but Looked to a Legendary Rolling Stone To Keep Going
With that, up-and-coming pop star Olivia Rodrigo has also introduced a more affordable tier of tickets. Since her fans skew younger, it makes so much sense for her to offer “Silver Star” priced random seats that only apply to a select amount of tickets available per show. Braverman told TWSJ that this blueprint established by The Rolling Stones sets a precedent that more acts are sure to follow: “It’s not a ton in most cases, but it’s enough to make the program meaningful.”
